# MODIFIED MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD AND MODIFIED MOMENT ESTIMATORS FOR THE THREE-PARAMETER WEIBULL DISTRIBUTION
A. Clifford Cohen and Betty Whitten
The University of Georgia Athens, Georgia 30602
Key Words and Phrases: modified estimators; maximum likelihood estimators; moment estimators; Monte Carlo study; life span distributions.

This article is concerned with modifications of both maximum likelihood and moment estimators for parameters of the three-parameter Weibull distribution. Modifications presented here are basically the same as those previously proposed by the authors (1980, 1981, 1982) in connection with the lognormal and the gamma distributions. Computer programs were prepared for the practical application of these estimators and an illustrative example is included. Results of a simulation study provide insight into the sampling behavior of the new estimators and include comparisons with the traditional moment and maximum likelihood estimators. For some combinations of parameter values, some of the modified estimators considered here enjoy advantages over both moment and maximum likelihood estimators with respect to bias, variance, and/or ease of calculation.
The Weibull distribution is widely employed as a model for distributions of life spans and reaction times. From a computational point of view, it is particularly appealing since its

cumulative distribution function can be expressed explicitly as a simple function of the random variable. Both two and three parameter Weibull distributions have been studied extensively by numerous writers including Cohen (1965, 1973, 1975), Dubey (1966), Harter and Moore (1965, 1967), Bain (1978), Mann (1968), Mann and Fertig (1975a, 1975b), Lemon (1974), Wingo (1973), Ringer and Sprinkle (1972), Rockette (1974), Zanakis (1977, 1979a, 1979b), Zanakis and Mann (1981), Wycoff, Bain, and Englehardt (1980), Königer (1981), and various others.

Moment estimators (ME) and maximum likelihood estimators (MLE) have been considered by most of these previous writers to be the traditional or standard estimators for parameters of this distribution. It is well known, however, that for some combinations of parameter values, maximum likelihood estimation in the three-parameter Weibull does not satisfy the usual regularity conditions and consequently can give rise to estimates not having the usual asymptotic properties and even to inconsistent estimates. For some samples, maximum likelihood estimates simply fail to exist. When any of these conditions prevail, the modified estimators presented in this article provide alternatives which often enjoy advantages over both moment and maximum likelihood estimators. In most instances modified estimates are easier to calculate and frequently exhibit smaller biases and variances than the maximum likelihood estimates. The estimators proposed here for the Weibull parameters are similar to those previously proposed by the authors (1980, 1981, 1982) for parameters of the lognormal and the gamma distributions. Consideration here is limited to complete samples. Estimation based on censored samples was previously studied by Cohen (1965 and 1975).

Although the Weibull distribution is usually perceived to be positively skewed, it becomes negatively skewed when  $\delta > \delta_0 = 3.6023494257197$  (Cohen, 1973). It is, of course, positively skewed when  $\delta < \delta_0$  and there is no skewness  $(\alpha_{3:x} = 0)$  when  $\delta = \delta_0$ . In applications concerning life spans and reaction times, values of  $\delta$  in excess of 3.22 ( $\alpha_{3:x} < 0.10$ ) seldom occur. However, in other applications larger values of  $\delta$  are sometimes encountered. Excellent expository accounts of this distribution and its applications have been given by Johnson and Kotz (1970) and by Mann, Schafer and Singpurwalla (1974).

When  $\delta > 1$ , the Weibull distribution is bell-shaped and maximum likelihood estimators can be found by simultaneously solving the system of equations obtained by equating to zero the partial derivatives of the log likelihood function with respect to the parameters. Computational problems are likely to be encountered when  $\delta$  is near to 1, even though  $\delta$  actually exceeds 1. Furthermore, the usual asymptotic properties of MLE do not hold unless  $\delta > 2$ . As a practical matter, it is not considered advisable to employ the MLE for parameters of the three-parameter Weibull distribution unless there is reason to expect that  $\delta > 2.2$ . Most of the calculations required in practical applications of estimators presented here can be performed on a hand-held calculator by using tables of the gamma, digamma and trigamma functions such as those given by Abramowitz and Stegun (1964). Some of the programmable hand-held calculators can be programmed to calculate these functions and thereby eliminate dependency on tables. Although standard iterative procedures might be employed, simple "trial and error" techniques coupled with linear interpolation are adequate for solving the various estimating equations. However, in order to facilitate routine calculation of estimates, a FORTRAN software package similar to those previously developed by the authors (1980, 1981, 1982) for parameters of the lognormal and gamma distributions, was prepared. This package was used to produce the simulation summaries contained in Tables II and III. (Computer listings of this package may be obtained from the authors.)

The BASIC module provides input for both the MLE and the MOMENT modules. The two latter modules are designed to solve applicable estimating equations iteratively for admissible estimates. For the maximum likelihood estimators and the modified maximum likelihood estimators, rules of admissibility require that  $\hat{\gamma} < x_1$ , and this restriction was incorporated into the MLE module. However, this restriction is not imposed on the moment and modified moment estimators. These estimators may therefore occasionally produce estimates of  $\gamma$  which are greater than  $x_1$ . In order to reduce computer time, a further restriction is imposed on the MLE and its modifications which requires that estimates of  $\gamma$  fall within an interval extending from a lower limit that is ten standard deviations below the sample mean to an upper limit that is no greater than  $x_1 - 10^{-4}$ . When a maximum likelihood or modified maximum likelihood estimate of  $\gamma$  falls outside this interval, such an occurrence should be interpreted as a suggestion that the Weibull distribution might not be the most appropriate model for the data under consideration. This restriction does not apply to the moment or modified moment estimators.

Additional restrictions were imposed on estimates of  $\delta$ . For the MLE, it is required that  $\hat{\delta}$  fall in the interval (1.01, 15.0) while for all other estimators it is required that  $\hat{\delta}$  fall in the interval (0.1, 15.0). The upper limit is somewhat arbitrary and can easily be adjusted to fit the needs of the user. For users whose data are fitted by distributions that are positively skewed, an upper limit of 3.6 might be considered since when  $\hat{\delta} = 3.6$  the third standard moment is approximately 0. When restrictions on  $\hat{\gamma}$  and/or  $\hat{\delta}$  are violated, calculations are terminated, and an appropriate message is printed for the user. The necessity for restrictions such as those imposed here has also been noted by Zanakis (1977).

A dichotomous search technique is employed in solving applicable estimating equations in both the MOMENT and MLE modules. For ME, and MME I-III, solutions to the third equation of (4.1), and solutions to equations (4.5), (4.7), and (4.9) are sought by first substituting  $\hat{\delta}_{i} - .01$  into the appropriate equation and incrementing  $\hat{\delta}_{j}$  by intervals of 0.1 until a solution is determined to be between  $\hat{\delta}_{i}$  and  $\hat{\delta}_{i-1}$ . At this time a binary search for the solution to the appropriate equation is undertaken. In order to control computer time cost, an effort is made to find solutions correct to  $10^{-5}$  within 50 iterations. Having found an estimate for  $\delta$ , estimates for  $\gamma$  and  $\beta$  are easily calculated from equations (4.2) and (4.3).

For MLE and MMLE I-V, estimates of  $\delta$  using equations (2.4), (3.4), (3.6), (3.7), (3.8), and (3.9) are calculated for specific values of  $\hat{\gamma}$ . The procedure used in searching for an estimate of  $\delta$  for each specific value of  $\hat{\gamma}$  is the same as that used in MOMENT. Having found an estimate of  $\delta$  for a given  $\hat{\gamma}$ , equation (2.5) is employed to calculate  $\hat{\beta}$ . The search for estimates  $\hat{\delta}, \hat{\gamma}$ , and  $\hat{\beta}$  begins with  $\hat{\gamma} = x_1 - 10^{-4}$  and continues with  $\hat{\gamma}$  being decremented until we find two values  $\gamma_i$  and  $\gamma_j$  such that  $(\partial \ln L \partial \gamma)_i \leq 0 \leq (\partial \ln L / \partial \gamma)_j$ . Having found an upper and lower limit on  $\hat{\gamma}$ , a binary search is employed to calculate final estimates of  $\gamma$  which in turn are employed to calculate final estimates for  $\delta$  and  $\beta$ .

A Monte Carlo study was undertaken in order to compare estimators with respect to their sampling behavior. One hundred random samples consisting of one hundred observations each were generated from Weibull populations for which  $\delta = 4.5$ , 2.2156, 1.5639, 1.2111, 1.0, and 0.8632. (These values correspond to  $\alpha_{3} = -0.1784$ , 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 and 2.5, respectively.) In addition 200 random samples consisting of 25 observations each were generated from populations in which  $\delta = 1.0$  and 0.8632. Ten samples of ten observations each were generated from a popu

lation in which  $\delta = 0.5$ . The terminus  $\gamma$  was set equal to 0, and the scale parameter  $\beta$  was set equal to 1, but in calculating estimates all three parameters were assumed to be unknown. Note that four of the populations sampled are bell-shaped ( $\delta > 1$ ) while three are reverse J-shaped ( $\delta < 1$ ).

The pseudo-random number generator RANF designed by CDC for the 60-bit word Cyber 70/74 computer was used in the simulation procedure to generate uniformly distributed random numbers. The multiplier for this generator passes the Coveyou-Macpherson test and other statistical tests for randomness including the autocorrelation test with lag  $\leq 100$  and the triplet test. Details concerning these tests are given in Fortran Version 5 Common Library Mathematical Routine Reference Manual (1981), Control Data Corp. Minneapolis, Mn. CDC Operating Systems: Nos. 1, Nos./BC1, Scope 2, #60483100.
The uniformly distributed random numbers thus generated were subsequently transformed to produce Weibull distributed random observations from each of the populations sampled.

The software package described in Section 7 was employed in an effort to calculate applicable estimates from each sample generated. Because of the previously described restrictions in the computer programs, some samples failed to produce estimates from some estimators. The means and standard deviations of estimates from each sequence of samples, together with counts of samples for which no estimates were found are entered in Tables II and III. All computations were performed at the University of Georgia Computer Center on a Cyber 70/74 computer.

The practical application of estimators presented in this paper is illustrated with a random sample consisting of 100 observations selected from a Weibull population in which  $\gamma = 0$ ,  $\beta = 1.0$ , and  $\delta = 1.5639$ . The population mean, standard deviation, third standard moment, and median are 0.8986, 0.5871, 1.0, and 0.7911 respectively. Individual sample observations are listed in Table V. For this sample,  $n = 100$ ,  $\overline{x} = 0.9602$ ,  $s = 0.5961$ ,  $a_3 = 1.0040$ ,  $m_{x} = 0.8477$ , and  $x_1 = 0.1009$ . The resulting estimates are displayed in Table VI. It is noted that for this sample, MME-I and MME-II yield estimates of  $\delta$  that are

in closest agreement with corresponding population values, while MME-III provides the closest estimate to the population value of  $\beta$  and MMLE-I provides the estimate of  $\gamma$  that is in closest agreement with the corresponding population value. However, the MME-I and MME-II estimates of  $\gamma$  are only slightly less favorable than the estimate obtained from MMLE-I.

An examination of the simulation summaries in Tables II and III discloses that when  $\delta \geq 2.2156 (\alpha_3 < 0.5)$ , the MLE performs well with respect to bias and variance. For  $\delta = 4.5$ , both the ME and MLE perform quite well in these respects. However when computing time is considered, we note that the MLE required considerably more time than the ME. When  $\delta \leq 2.2156$ , MME-I, MMLE-I and MMLE-II appear to be the preferred estimators.

When computing time is not at a premium, it is recommended that MMLE-I or MMLE-II be employed regardless of the value of  $\delta$ . If computing time is expensive, then it is recommended that MME-I be employed except in samples where skewness is near zero. In the latter situation the ME would be preferred over the modified estimators.

Both the ME and MME-I are easy to calculate on a simple hand-held calculator provided adequate tables of the gamma function are available. If a programmable hand-held calculator is available, the gamma function can be programmed and tables are not needed.
